title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair loop changes the verifier-detected safety-violation rate of LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. Following a preregistered paired design (N=500 intent→configuration tasks) we compared (1) baseline: a single LLM proposal (gpt-5-mini) and (2) guarded: the same LLM proposal screened by a deterministic netops validator with up to one automated repair iteration. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); absolute paired success-rate difference = 0.002; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.006]. Interpretation: on this synthetic, verifier-scoped corpus and this model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-perfect proposals, so the marginal verifier+repair effect on the measured pass rate was numerically small. We report preregistration, full execution manifest, and archived prompts/outputs; we add clarifications required by peer review about shared-generation semantics, model-call accounting, verifier scope, and observed repair activity.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as intent-to-configuration translation, change planning, and limited self-healing. Prior system and survey work emphasizes that operational reliability arises from the combination of model capability and surrounding engineering (validators, canarying, rollback, constrained workflows) rather than from the model alone [Beckett et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate–validate–repair (generate–critic) architectures are a suggested pattern to improve correctness of structured outputs, but controlled measurements that isolate the verifier contribution in an LLM-driven NetOps loop are scarce. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment to answer a focused question: How much does integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair loop reduce verifier-detected safety violations in LLM-generated device-configuration proposals, compared to LLM-only proposals, when tasks and topologies are canonical and restricted to verifier-modeled features? The paper reports the preregistered design, execution, and confirmatory analysis, and clarifies execution accounting and verifier scope as required for correct interpretation.
sections.related_work: Deterministic and formal network-verification approaches (header-space, route-model analyzers, Minesweeper-style tools) can check reachability, isolation, and other properties on configuration models [Beckett et al., 2017]. Recent NetOps/AIOps work integrates LLMs into intent-driven pipelines and emphasizes that validators and operational guardrails are essential for safe automation [Wang et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate–verify–repair loops have been examined in other structured domains (code, configuration, model repair) and are proposed for NetOps, but public, controlled ablations quantifying verifier effect size remain limited. Studies of LLM failure modes motivate guardrails: hallucination, overconfidence, and tool/encoding failures can produce hazardous operational recommendations absent validation [Owen, 2026]. Our study contributes a preregistered, paired measurement isolating verifier+repair impact under constrained synthetic conditions.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The experiment was preregistered (study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026) before execution; the preregistration artifact and frozen analysis plan are archived (preregistration SHA-256: 405a9f882cbf...). Confirmatory hypothesis: an LLM paired with a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration will produce a lower verifier-detected safety-violation rate than the same LLM producing a single proposal without verifier feedback (paired within-task comparison). Sampling and tasks: 500 deterministic synthetic intent→configuration tasks were generated deterministically and stratified across canonical clusters (VLAN-change, ACL-change, static-route-change) per the preregistration sampling plan; tasks that referenced features not modeled by the verifier were to be excluded from the primary analysis (no such exclusions occurred—see Results). Model and orchestration: LLM = gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses) called via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Generation semantics and model-call accounting (peer-review clarification): the preregistered transformation semantics used a single shared initial generation per task (generation_semantics = 'shared_initial_candidate', independent_condition_generation = false). Concretely, for each task one LLM proposal was generated and that same proposal was evaluated under both arms: baseline (the raw proposal considered as the baseline pipeline output) and guarded (the same proposal checked by the deterministic validator, with an automated repair iteration performed only if the validator reported preregistered high/medium-severity violations). This design isolates the verifier+repair effect conditional on the same initial candidate. Execution manifest accounting (artifact-backed fact): model_calls_used = 501; provider audit stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 500, repair: 1}; condition_counts = {shared:500, guarded:1} (execution manifest and deterministic reconciliation are archived). The single observed repair call corresponds to the single repair-stage provider call recorded in the manifest. Primary outcome and analysis: per-task binary outcome 'pass' == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations on the final configuration the validator models. Primary confirmatory test: exact McNemar two-sided test on paired pass/fail labels (alpha = 0.05); absolute and relative risk reduction reported with 95% CIs using paired bootstrap (B = 10000, seed = 1729). Missingness and exclusions: per preregistration missingness rules and deterministic retry policy were enforced; complete_pair_count = 500; no confirmatory pairs were excluded. Reproducibility: all prompts, model outputs, validator traces, seeds, and logs are archived in the execution evidence bundle (representative artifact hashes cited in the Disclosure).
sections.results: Execution summary (artifact-backed): the adapter completed the preregistered confirmatory run. Complete pairs = 500; model_calls_used = 501 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair = 1). Primary confirmatory outcomes (archived analysis results): baseline_success_count = 499 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded_success_count = 500 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). Paired contingency counts: n11 = 499 (both pass), n10 = 1 (guarded pass only), n01 = 0 (baseline pass only), n00 = 0 (both fail). Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0020000000000000018. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00. Paired-bootstrap 95% CI for the absolute difference = [0.0, 0.006] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Repair activity and exclusions: zero tasks were excluded from the primary confirmatory analysis for referencing unmodeled features (exclusions = []). The execution-manifest stage counts show exactly one repair-stage provider call across the full experiment; repair-stage invocation therefore was minimal. Interpretation of statistical outcome (peer-review clarification): the exact-McNemar p = 1.00 arises because only a single discordant pair was observed (n10 = 1, n01 = 0); with such extreme ceiling performance the two-sided exact test returns a non-significant result (p large), and the paired-bootstrap CI is consistent with a small non-negative effect up to 0.006. This pattern indicates a ceiling effect—very low baseline error prevalence—rather than evidence that verifiers are universally unnecessary. Secondary and exploratory diagnostics: repair-stage latency and per-task validator diagnostics are archived; repair-stage count = 1 (as above). Per-cluster breakdown artifacts are available in the evidence bundle; we do not report additional per-cluster summary numbers here beyond what is in the archived analysis artifacts to avoid reporting unregistered exploratory contrasts as confirmatory results.
sections.discussion: Practical reading: under the constrained synthetic corpus and verifier-modeled features the tested LLM produced near-perfect proposals (499/500 baseline passes), leaving little room for additional verifier+repair improvements in the measured pass-rate metric. The single discordant case shows that the guarded loop can correct rare baseline failures, and the verifier serves as a formal safety gate. However, measured verifier impact on this metric depends crucially on (a) initial LLM error prevalence on the evaluated task distribution and (b) the verifier's modeling coverage. Verifier modeling scope and its consequences (peer-review clarification): the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 validated the configuration semantics used by the synthetic task generator in this run; representative task payloads show the validator modeled interface-level fields used in these tasks (allowed_fields in representative task entries include admin, mtu, vlan) and workflow constraints expressed by the generator (see representative task entries in the evidence bundle). The validator did not stand in for full cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, nor for unmodeled protocol features outside the preregistered verifier scope; tasks referencing unmodeled features would have been excluded per the preregistration (none were in the confirmatory set). Limitations and external validity: the study used a synthetic deterministically generated corpus restricted to verifier-modeled features, a single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation; only one automated repair iteration was permitted per preregistration. These design choices were deliberate to make a focused, reproducible measurement of verifier impact under controlled conditions; they reduce external generality to unconstrained production settings, multi-vendor CLIs, or longer iterative repair budgets. Operational implication: organizations should evaluate guardrail investment relative to observed proposal error rates and verifier coverage; where initial proposal error rates are higher or verifier coverage broader, measured verifier impact is expected to be larger. Future work should vary model family, verifier scope, task realism (noisier intents, cross-vendor syntax), and repair budget to map verifier benefit across more operationally challenging regimes.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=500) comparing an LLM-only proposal pipeline to an LLM plus deterministic verifier and one repair iteration. Both arms achieved near-perfect verifier pass rates (baseline 499/500, guarded 500/500), producing an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00). The finding shows that, on a constrained synthetic corpus and within the verifier scope used here, a modern LLM can already produce operationally valid configurations and that measured verifier benefit on the pass-rate metric can be small when baseline error prevalence is very low. This does not negate the engineering value of verifiers; rather it quantifies a ceiling-effect regime where guardrail marginal utility is small. Practitioners should measure proposal error rates and verifier coverage on their realistic workloads to prioritize guardrail investments and should examine verifier impact under broader, noisier, and cross-vendor conditions in future studies.

limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; results do not necessarily generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or to protocol semantics outside the verifier scope (representative task payloads show allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}).
Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini) — no claim of multi-model generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted; different repair budgets or iterative repair strategies may change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) creates a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the observed non-significant exact-McNemar p = 1.00 should be interpreted in that context rather than as evidence that verifiers are universally unnecessary.
